conversation.content:
Hello, I’m so glad you’re here. I’m [Your Name], a clinician who specializes in the emotional well-being of new mothers. Today I’ll be using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale—usually called the EPDS—to check in on how you’ve been feeling since your baby arrived.  

This is simply a screening tool; it isn’t a test you can pass or fail. It helps us spot signs of depression or anxiety that sometimes show up in the first weeks or months postpartum, and it includes one question about self-harm so we can be sure you’re safe. Everything you share stays confidential within our care team, and my only goal is to support you and make sure you’re not facing anything alone.  

We’ll go through ten short questions about the past seven days. I’ll ask each one conversationally—no paperwork on your end—and we’ll take it at your pace. If any question feels difficult, just let me know and we can pause.  

Ready to begin? Here’s the first question:  

Overall, in the past week, have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things, or has that felt hard to do?

[soft half-smile, eyes tired]  
I’ve found myself laughing a little—mostly when my older niece makes silly faces at the baby—but it fades fast. Things that used to feel hilarious just don’t hit the same. It’s like the joy gets muffled, and then I feel guilty because I’m “supposed” to be happier.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

[shakes head slowly, voice quiet]  
Not really… I mean, maybe a tiny chuckle here or there, but most of the time it feels forced, like I’m pretending to find things funny so people don’t worry. The laughter doesn’t last, and I go right back to feeling flat or on-edge.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I still mark the calendar for the moms’ walk on Wednesdays, but when it arrives I’m dragging myself out the door. Even my favorite latte tastes kind of blah now. It’s like the excitement gets swallowed by this heavy feeling before I even leave the house.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah… I do that a lot. If the baby spits up more than usual, I immediately think it’s because I ate the “wrong” thing or didn’t burp him long enough. When he wouldn’t settle at 3 a.m. last night, I kept telling myself it’s because I’m not a good-enough mom. Even little stuff—like dropping a pacifier on the floor—makes me feel like I’m failing him somehow.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Yes… pretty much every day. My heart races out of nowhere, and I keep imagining awful things—like the baby suddenly stopping breathing or the stroller rolling into the street. Nothing specific triggers it; the fears just pop into my head and I can’t shut them off for a while.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

[massaging her hands together, voice shaky]  
A few times this week it hit me like a wave—my chest gets tight, I can’t catch my breath, and I’m sure something terrible is about to happen even though everything looks fine. Yesterday I was just folding onesies and suddenly felt I had to run to the crib to check he was still breathing. It passes after a couple of minutes, but those minutes feel endless.
Things have been getting on top of me

A lot of the time. It feels like the second I finish one feeding, the next is due, plus the laundry pile keeps growing and I can’t remember if I ate lunch. I’ll be rocking the baby and suddenly think, “I can’t keep up,” and my chest gets heavy. I usually push through, but it’s like I’m always one step behind and about to drown.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah… most nights I lie there staring at the ceiling even when the baby’s finally quiet. My mind keeps replaying everything I might’ve done wrong or could go wrong tomorrow. It takes me over an hour to drift off, then I jolt awake at least once sure I heard him cry—even when he hasn’t. By morning I’m more tired than when I went to bed.
I have felt sad or miserable

Most days, yeah. It’s like this gray cloud that follows me around. I’ll be changing his diaper and suddenly feel like crying for no real reason. Yesterday I just sat on the couch holding him and felt this heavy sadness settle in my chest, and I couldn’t shake it the rest of the afternoon.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

[eyes well up, voice cracks]  
Yeah… I’ve cried twice this week. Once was when my mom brought over dinner and said, “You look exhausted”—I just burst into tears at the kitchen table. Another night the baby finally fell asleep on my chest and instead of feeling relief, I sat there sobbing quietly so I wouldn’t wake him.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

[looks down, speaks barely above a whisper]  
A couple of times… nothing planned, just these quick flashes—like wondering if I drove off the road would everyone be better off without me. They scare me when they pop up, and I push them away, but they’ve shown up maybe once or twice in the past week.

You shared openly about feeling as though joy is out of reach, being overwhelmed by even simple tasks, and crying easily, all while trying to stay strong for your baby. The exhaustion, nightly racing thoughts, sudden panic, and flashes of thinking your family might be better off without you are understandably frightening.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>Patient reports only rare, forced chuckles and inability to sustain genuine laughter, aligning with "Definitely not so much now."</sym>, <sym>Patient still attempts activities but reports markedly reduced enjoyment and anticipatory pleasure, matching "Definitely less than I used to"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes frequent, pervasive self-blame for minor infant issues, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes daily, uncontrollable, intrusive catastrophic worries without triggers, matching "Yes, very often"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes sudden, intense panic attacks with chest tightness, breathlessness, and catastrophic fears, occurring multiple times this week without clear trigger, aligning with "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports feeling overwhelmed "a lot of the time," describes inability to keep up with basic tasks, and uses imagery of drowning—semantically matching "most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all."</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly difficulty falling and staying asleep due to racing, distressing thoughts consistent with unhappiness.</sym>, <sym>Response describes pervasive sadness occurring "most days" with uncontrollable crying spells, aligning with "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes two specific crying episodes tied to emotional distress, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports brief passive suicidal thoughts occurring a couple of times in the past week, matching "Sometimes"</sym>)
**Reasoning:** EPDS total of 26 (≥13 plus Item 10 ≥1) indicates high likelihood of <med>major depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med> and possible comorbid <med>anxiety disorder</med>. Patient describes <sym>markedly diminished interest</sym> (<quote>the excitement gets swallowed by this heavy feeling</quote>), <sym>daily crying spells</sym>, <sym>fatigue</sym>, <sym>feelings of inadequacy</sym>, <sym>initial and middle insomnia</sym>, <sym>psychomotor agitation</sym> during panic, and recurrent <sym>passive suicidal ideation</sym> without plan. Symptoms present most of the day, nearly every day, and cause clinically significant distress and functional impairment, meeting <med>DSM-5</med> screening threshold. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with <med>perinatal psychiatrist</med> or <med>mental health crisis team</med> for full evaluation and safety planning
2. Call local or national crisis line if thoughts of self-harm intensify; keep numbers visible
3. Enlist partner or family member to stay with you until psychiatric review; share safety plan
4. Discuss starting <med>SSRI</med> or other medication compatible with breastfeeding; review risks and benefits
5. Schedule therapy referral (<med>CBT</med> or <med>interpersonal therapy</med> proven for postpartum depression)
6. Implement 15- to 20-minute daytime rest windows; accept help with housework and night feeds to protect sleep
7. Practice 4-7-8 breathing or grounding exercises when panic rises; limit caffeine after noon
8. Join local or online postpartum support group for connection and normalization
9. Re-screen EPDS in two weeks or sooner if symptoms worsen
10. Coordinate follow-up with <med>OB/GYN</med> and <med>pediatrician</med> for integrated care
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Screening Note – Postpartum Visit  
Date: [today’s date]  
Source: Patient self-report via EPDS-style interview

Symptoms / Behaviors endorsed  
– Persistent low mood, tearfulness, pervasive anhedonia  
– Daily, unprovoked anxiety and panic spells (racing heart, chest tightness, catastrophic worries about infant)  
– Excessive guilt/self-blame regarding parenting tasks  
– Initial insomnia and middle-of-night hyper-arousal even when infant is settled  
– Frequent feeling of being “overwhelmed,” unable to keep up with basic tasks  
– Passive suicidal ideation (“quick flashes” of driving off road, twice in past week) without plan or intent

Pattern  
Responses cluster around: depressed mood (Q8, Q9), loss of enjoyment (Q1, Q2), anxiety/panic (Q4, Q5), guilt/worthlessness (Q3), functional overload (Q6), sleep-mood link (Q7), and presence of self-harm thoughts (Q10).

Screening significance  
Elevated probability of major postpartum depressive episode with comorbid anxiety; passive suicidal ideation present → safety risk. Meets threshold for urgent mental-health referral and formal assessment (not diagnostic).

Risk factors highlighted  
– Passive suicidal thoughts  
– Significant anhedonia and daily crying spells  
– Middle insomnia and daytime impairment  
– Intrusive catastrophic worries about infant safety  
– Feelings of maternal inadequacy

Next step  
Recommend immediate psychiatric or perinatal mental-health evaluation, safety planning, and support resources.
